subject: feat(io): refresh vended storage credentials per prefix (#892)
body:
Vended storage credentials can expire while an `ArrowS3FileIO` instance and its
file handles are still in use. This change refreshes them on demand and keeps
the refresh state scoped to each storage prefix.

The implementation:

- Keeps one `CredentialStore` for credential snapshots, per-prefix slots,
  expiry state, refresh coordination, backoff, and generation checks.
- Resolves each credential once into its normalized prefix, effective client
  properties, client settings, and AWS credentials.
- Refreshes credentials independently by prefix. A response may update the
  prefixes that are still active; invalid, expired, missing, or incompatible
  entries keep their previous state.
- Preserves S3-compatible schemes during routing. For example, `s3://` and
  `oss://` remain separate prefixes so credentials for one endpoint cannot be
  sent to another.
- Lets existing AWS SDK clients pick up refreshed credentials through
  `AWSCredentialsProvider`, while keeping clients and handles safe when the
  `FileIO` or a credential generation is replaced.
- Uses the REST client connection and request timeout properties for all HTTP
  methods. Transport failures during table creation or commit are reported as
  `CommitStateUnknown` because the server may already have applied the write.

The change removes the previous global expiry/layout bookkeeping and duplicate
credential-property parsing, making the refresh path easier to maintain and
extend while preserving the existing `StorageCredentialProvider` API.

Tests cover prefix routing, refresh timing and concurrency, failed and invalid
refreshes, reordered responses, expiry handling, REST client timeouts, and
real S3-compatible round trips.

subject: fix(catalog): validate namespace existence in InMemoryCatalog create and register (#980)
body:
## What

`InMemoryCatalog` did not correctly check that a table's namespace exists, in two methods.

`CreateTable` wrote the table metadata file before validating the namespace. Creating a table under a missing namespace returned `kNoSuchNamespace`, but on object-store `FileIO` it first left an orphaned `00000-<uuid>.metadata.json` that nothing later removes, and on the default local `FileIO` the stray write failed with a misleading `kIOError`.

`RegisterTable` guarded with `if (!root_namespace_->NamespaceExists(identifier.ns))`. `NamespaceExists` returns `Result<bool>`, so `!result` tests `has_value()` rather than the bool, and a missing namespace is a value `false`, not an error. The branch was dead code, and a missing namespace surfaced as `kUnknownError` instead of `kNoSuchNamespace`.

Closes #977.

## How

`CreateTable` now validates the namespace before writing any metadata, matching `SqlCatalog::CreateTable`. `RegisterTable` reads the metadata outside the lock, then validates the namespace and registers under a single lock: the dead `if (!NamespaceExists(...))` check (which tested the `Result<bool>`'s `has_value()` rather than the contained bool) becomes an unwrap that returns `kNoSuchNamespace`. Keeping the namespace check and the registration in one critical section leaves them atomic, and the metadata read stays off the lock. The empty (root) namespace still resolves to `true`, so ordinary table creation is unaffected.

## Testing

Two new tests in `in_memory_catalog_test.cc`:

- `CreateTableNonexistentNamespace` — creating a table under a missing namespace returns `kNoSuchNamespace` and leaves no metadata file behind. It passes an explicit location whose `metadata/` directory already exists, so the pre-fix write lands a detectable orphan there; the zero-file assertion is what fails without the fix. The error-kind assertion alone would still pass pre-fix, because the later `UpdateTableMetadataLocation` also returns `kNoSuchNamespace` after the orphan is written.
- `RegisterTableNonexistentNamespace` — registering under a missing namespace returns `kNoSuchNamespace`; without the fix the dead `Result<bool>` check let it fall through to `kUnknownError`.

subject: fix(io): attempt every S3 delete and report how many failed (#966)
body:
Follow-up to https://github.com/apache/iceberg-cpp/pull/898#discussion_r4091927837.

`ArrowS3FileIO::DeleteFiles` returned at the first credential prefix whose delete failed, so files under the remaining prefixes were never attempted. It now attempts every file unless task submission fails, logs deletion failures, and returns `Failed to delete N of M files`. Exceptions thrown by individual deletes are counted too.

- Deletion is sequential by default. `InitializeS3FileIODeleteExecutor(Executor*)` initializes a caller-owned executor shared by all S3 FileIOs, including registry-created instances. Initialize it before the first delete; otherwise, the first delete freezes the default `nullptr`. Repeating the same pointer is allowed, but replacing it is not. The executor must remain alive until the last delete completes.
- `s3.delete.num-threads` limits worker tasks per call, defaulting to the hardware thread count. Workers share a file index, keeping task/future storage bounded by the configured parallelism. The shared executor controls total concurrency; this property does not create or resize a thread pool.
- Accepted tasks finish before the call exits, including when submission returns an error or throws. Submission failures are returned without falling back to the calling thread and bypassing the executor's concurrency limit. All workers use the same delegate snapshot and the caller's logger.

Arrow has no public S3 batch-delete API, so each request still deletes one file. `ResolvingFileIO` keeps its existing fail-fast behavior across delegates.

Tests cover deletion across allowed/denied prefixes, thrown deletes, rejected/throwing submissions, bounded task counts and concurrency, immutable executor initialization, and executor configuration for both direct and registry-created FileIOs.

subject: fix(metadata): write and detect gzip-compressed table metadata (#1014)
body:
Codec::FromFileName used find_last_of with the multi-character suffix
'.metadata.json', which matches the last single character of the set
(the final 'n') instead of the suffix. For gzip-compressed metadata
written by Iceberg Java as '<name>.gz.metadata.json', the resulting
file_name_without_suffix kept the wrong tail, the '.gz' check failed,
and the file was misclassified as uncompressed kNone. Reading such a
file then fails to decompress.

Use rfind so the whole suffix matches. The legacy '.metadata.json.gz'
compatibility branch is unchanged. Round-trip reading of Java-written
gzip metadata files is covered by new unit tests.

NewTableMetadataFilePath names the file '<version>-<uuid>.gz.metadata.json'
when write.metadata.compression-codec is gzip, but Write always emitted plain
JSON, so the file contradicted its own name and no reader could inflate it.
Add a GZipCompressor next to the existing GZipDecompressor and compress in
Write when the location's codec is gzip, completing the round trip.

subject: feat: add CherryPickOperation and wire SnapshotManager::Cherrypick (#926)
body:
Adds `CherryPickOperation` and implements `SnapshotManager::Cherrypick()`, which was a TODO stub.

Follows Java's `CherryPickOperation`: appends re-apply their added files, dynamic overwrites (`replace-partitions`) re-apply adds and deletes and are rejected if a replaced partition changed, and anything else can only be fast-forward. Records `source-snapshot-id` and `published-wap-id`, and rejects a WAP id that was already published.

Like Java, the operation is reachable only through `Transaction`, not `Table`.

Fast-forwards also follow Java: `Apply()` returns the picked snapshot itself when it is a child of the current state, so no new snapshot is created. Because that decision is re-evaluated on every apply, a commit retry against moved metadata replays the pick on top of the new state instead of being rejected.

Tests ported from Java `TestSnapshotManager` and `TestWapWorkflow`, plus regression coverage for commit retries and the fast-forward/replay transitions.

Part of #637.

subject: fix(bucket): reject oversized input in BucketUtils::HashBytes (#961)
body:
* fix(bucket): reject oversized input in BucketUtils::HashBytes

HashBytes passed a size_t length straight to the vendored
MurmurHash3_x86_32, whose length parameter is a signed 32-bit int. For
inputs of 2^31 bytes or more the length wrapped negative, making the
hash loop read far out of bounds (and nblocks * 4 signed-overflow UB);
for inputs above 2^32 bytes a silently wrong prefix was hashed, breaking
the bucket contract against other implementations.

Every literal hash path (kDecimal/kString/kUuid/kBinary/kFixed) funnels
through this one function, so guard it there: reject lengths above
INT32_MAX with ICEBERG_CHECK_OR_DIE before the narrowing cast. The bound
matches the limit implied by iceberg-java's byte arrays, so no legal
bucket input is rejected. The vendored murmurhash3_internal.cc is left
untouched (tagged third-party code) and the now-checked narrowing is
made explicit with static_cast<int>.

Add BucketUtilsTest.HashBytesRejectsOversizedInput, which fabricates an
oversized span over a 1-byte buffer (never dereferenced, so no 2 GiB
allocation is needed in CI). Without the guard the test segfaults.

* test(bucket): guard raw byte input so the oversized-length test is well-formed

The regression test built a std::span over INT32_MAX + 1 elements of a
one-byte object, which violates the std::span constructor precondition and
is undefined behavior even though the data is never read.

Move the length guard into an internal HashBytes(const uint8_t*, size_t)
overload and keep BucketUtils::HashBytes(std::span) as a thin wrapper, so the
test can pass a null pointer with the oversized length instead.

Also document that HashBytes and BucketIndex throw IcebergError for inputs
larger than INT32_MAX, which the public headers did not mention.

---------
